messages.subject_clean: D-RUG Code of Conduct
messages.body_plain:
Dear D-RUG community,

We strive to make D-RUG an open and inclusive community to all who wish to be involved. Given recent events <https://noamross.github.io/datacamp-sexual-assault/> that have occurred within the data science community, we wanted to take the opportunity to establish a Code of Conduct for the Davis R Users Group <https://d-rug.github.io/code-of-conduct.html>. Although these rules have implicitly governed our community since its inception, we wanted to make this Code of Conduct explicit to better support and strengthen our community.

As a combined physical and virtual community, we recognize that we may be limited in how we can enforce Code of Conduct violations that occur outside of the physical space of UC Davis. Still, we wish to make the enforcement mechanisms clear, and ask that our community help in keeping everyone accountable.

We hope that this Code of Conduct aids in our continued efforts to foster a supportive community for folks to learn and grow as R Users.

Sincerely,
Taylor, Ryan, Martha, & Michael

messages.subject_clean: [D-RUG]: secondary axis with facet wrap
messages.body_plain:
Look at facet_grid() if you want another another dimension on another axis for the facets.

If you want another another dimension on the same axis, use + between your variables, i.e. facet_wrap(dim_1 + dim_2~.). You can also combine facet_grid and +, though it might become too much at the end.

Does this answer your question?
library(ggplot2)
#> Registered S3 methods overwritten by 'ggplot2':
#>   method         from
#>   [.quosures     rlang
#>   c.quosures     rlang
#>   print.quosures rlang

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(cyl~ drv)

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(cyl+ drv~.)

ggplot(mpg, aes(displ, hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(cyl +fl~ drv)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Davis R Users,

I suspect that the following question is unanswerable without actually modifying the source code of randomForest to save individual variable importance measures per CART model, but maybe I’m wrong.

Basically, I’m looking for a way to obtain individual variable importance on a tree-by-tree basis rather than the summarized output of importance(my_rf_model). I would like this so I can make cumulative variable importance animations directly from randomForestobjects (see animation below with mtcars).

If you think this is a good question, please consider upvoting it on stack overflow to give it more attention <https://stackoverflow.com/questions/55985294/obtain-importance-of-individual-trees-in-a-randomforest>, and if you know an answer, that’s even better!

Regards,
Rich

Hi

I am wondering whether anyone here played once trying to get a nice UC Davis-like color palette for plotting graphs? I found UC Davis colors definition here <https://marketingtoolbox.ucdavis.edu/visual-identity/color.html>, they give also lighter shades of their blue and yellow. I realize any attempt to define a custom palette raises issues that the result might not be state of the art (perception-neutral, color-blind-safe etc) but I am ready to compromise (some) science for aesthetics.

I am mainly looking for a qualitative one (for sequential, could just use their lighter shades?). Thinking of mixing 1-2 blues and 1-2 yellows, though result could be heavily "perception non-neutral" ? See below my first attempt.

Another approach could be to simply look for existing palettes that resemble the UC Davis colors. On the sequential side, I feel the viridis one is a close match!?

Thanks!

Matthieu

library(ggplot2)
#> Registered S3 methods overwritten by 'ggplot2':

#>   c.quosures     rlang
#>   print.quosures rlang

cols <- c("#DAAA00", "#002855", "#E9CC66", "#667D9D")
seq_cols <- seq_len(length(cols))

qplot(x=seq_cols, y= seq_cols, geom="col", fill= factor(seq_cols)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols)

Hi Matthieu,

Colorate helps generate nice palettes given a specific color. Here's an example with the yellow you provided:
http://colorate.azurewebsites.net/Color/DAAA00

Chroma.js is also great for generating balanced, multi-hued sequential/diverging palettes (https://www.vis4.net/blog/2013/09/mastering-multi-hued-color-scales/). The nice thing about it is that you can specify the number and types of colors you want. So you can combine colorate's suggestions with chroma's palette generation, using UC Davis' colors as a reference.

e.g. https://gka.github.io/palettes/#colors=#002855,#DAAA00|steps=7|bez=1|coL=1 <https://gka.github.io/palettes/#colors=%23002855,%23DAAA00%7Csteps=7%7Cbez=1%7CcoL=1>

Hope that's helpful!

Best,
Nistara

messages.body_plain:
I strongly advocate for Blogdown/Hugo + Netlify route. The templates are very nice and easy to use and you're spot on with your terminology for hosting/deploying. I know Xie's blogdown book was written with Alison Hill, and all the content on how to get up and running is in there, but I found that the book is too technical for a true beginner. It's a great reference for once you have your feet wet a little bit. I would refer you to Alison's walk through to get started:  https://alison.rbind.io/post/up-and-running-with-blogdown/

My academic website (www.norcalbiostat.com <http://www.norcalbiostat.com/>) uses the blogdown/hugo setup, stored in github and hosted via netlify.  I really like the flexibility that I have for each section.

However for each of my individual course websites (you can find under teaching), all use static Rmarkdown files, and are hosted on Github directly. They are *great* for a simple website with not a lot of moving parts i.e. like a blog. I am pretty happy with the balance and I like keeping them (overall website vs class website)

My main advice is to stick with one of the three templates that Xie references in the book, and don't get caught up in the customizing theme hell until you really know what you want and where you want it. Don't expect to get it right the first time, and don't feel bad if you have to burn it all down and start over.

I will be reworking the Data Science Initiative website (datascience.csuchico.edu <http://datascience.csuchico.edu>) over this summer to have less of a blog-centric feel to it, so I'll be having blogdown on the brain for a while. I would be happy to try to field any questions you may have.

-Robin

Hi Esther,
I've been using Jekyll + Github and Rmarkdown sites for awhile now, and it's worked pretty well. I know blogdown is a pretty slick way to go now, and in combo with Hugo, I'd say that's probably going to be your best bet. However, Jekyll isn't going anywhere and there's plenty of websites (and tutorials) that are based on Jekyll. One thing to consider is if you don't want something fancy, you could use a simple Rmarkdown/Github website, which doesn't require dealing with jekyll or hugo (see the R-DAVIS website as an example: https://gge-ucd.github.io/R-DAVIS/...it's all built in Rmarkdown/RStudio and hosted on Github).

If you want something with a little more flexibility and more options, then probably going Hugo/Jekyll is best, especially now that blogdown is well supported and there's a good amount of documentation.

Not sure if that helps, but that's my two cents. Martha gave a nice presentation on website building (mainly following the simplest Rmarkdown/Github option) at D-RUG a little while ago, the presentation is here: https://d-rug.github.io/blog/2018/Martha-Wohlfeil-building-a-website.

My personal website uses Jekyll, and I followed Dean Attali's Beautiful Jekyll template <https://deanattali.com/beautiful-jekyll/>, and it wasn't to hard to get things all set up and running (hosted via Github).

I'm sure other folks may have more tips/advice.

Adios,
Ryan
